cards.prompt:
A spam filter learns from messages people have already labelled **spam** or **not spam**. In this one's examples, **"free"** only ever appeared in spam: "Win a free phone", "Free prize", "Claim your free gift card".

Your friend texts **"Free pizza at footy training"**. Will the filter call it spam?

options.text: Yes: in its examples, "free" has only ever meant spam
No: it can tell the message comes from a friend
options.nudge: The filter only sees the words, and all it knows about them comes from its examples. What did those teach it about "free"?

options.text: No: it knows people say "free pizza" all the time
options.nudge: It only knows what its examples showed it. Did any of them use "free" in a friendly way?

options.text: It can't guess: it has never seen this exact message
options.nudge: Guessing about new things is a model's whole job. It uses the patterns in its examples. What pattern does "free" follow there?

cards.hint: The filter knows nothing except its examples. Look at which kind of message "free" turned up in.
cards.explanation: To this filter, **"free" means spam**, because that's all its examples ever showed. Real friends say "free" too (free time, free tickets), but a model can't learn from examples it never saw. Next, watch it happen.

cards.prompt: A spam filter learns from messages people have labelled. Label each message as **spam** or **not spam**. Then press Check to train the [[model]] and see what it makes of two new messages.

examples.text: Your parcel is held, pay the fee here
examples.label: spam

examples.text: Can you send me the homework
examples.label: ok

tests.text: Click to claim a free prize

cards.hint: Spam tries to get you to win, claim, click or pay. Normal messages are about plans and everyday things.
cards.nudge: Look again at the messages about prizes, gift cards and paying a fee: who sends those?
cards.explanation: Your labels were right. The model caught the prize message, but it also called **"Free pizza at footy training"** spam. In its examples, "free" only ever appeared in spam.

cards.title: Words that vote
cards.body:
So how did it decide? In this model, words **vote**. Each word of 3 or more letters gets one vote for every training message it was in, for that message's label.

"Free" was in three spam messages: 3 votes for spam. "Pizza" and "training" gave not spam just 2. Most votes wins; a tie means "not sure".

cards.prompt: The model only went wrong because nobody friendly in its examples ever said "free". Choose which examples to train on, so it gets **both** test messages right.

examples.text: Your parcel is held, pay the fee here
examples.label: spam

examples.text: Can you send me the homework
examples.label: ok

tests.text: Click to claim a free prize

cards.hint: Which side needs more votes from "free"? Look for an example where a friend says it.
cards.nudge: Watch the guess for the pizza message as you tick and untick. A tie shows as "Not sure", which isn't right yet.
cards.explanation: Adding **"Free footy training on Saturday"** shows the model that friends say "free" too, so the pizza message gets more not-spam votes. Deleting spam examples can also flip it, but then the model learns less about real spam. "Pizza, pizza, pizza!" adds just one vote: a word counts once per message.

cards.prompt: Good training data has **checked labels**, **lots of variety**, and examples like the ones the model will really meet. Does each one make training data **better**, or cause a **problem**?

items.label: Messages from lots of different people
Labels checked by a second person
Examples like the ones it will meet
Labels done in a rush, never checked

cards.hint: Ask of each one: does it teach the model something new and true?
cards.nudge: Look for the ones that teach the model something wrong, repeat one example over and over, or leave whole groups out.
cards.explanation: Variety, checked labels and realistic examples make data **better**. Rushed labels and spam marked "not spam" teach wrong lessons. A thousand copies add nothing new and tip the votes. One office leaves everyone else out.

cards.prompt: Someone made a labelling mistake in this fruit data. Find it, and choose the examples to train on so the model gets **both** test fruits right. (This model picks the **nearest** example.)
cards.hint: Read each example's name and the label beside it. Does every label match its name?
cards.nudge: Check that every example's label matches its name.
cards.explanation: "Long banana" was labelled **Apple**. It sat closest to the ripe banana, so the model copied its wrong label. Leaving that one example out fixes it: one wrong label can be enough to cause a mistake.

cards.prompt: A spam filter learned only from **English** messages. It lets lots of **Spanish** spam through. Which **one** addition helps most?

options.nudge: That's a lot more data, but does any of it show the model Spanish spam?

options.text: 200 Spanish messages, spam and normal, labelled
200 Spanish spam messages, all labelled spam
options.nudge: Close! But if every Spanish message it sees is spam, what will it think of a friend writing in Spanish?
Copies add nothing new. What's missing from its examples?

cards.hint: Think about what's missing from its examples, and what would happen to normal messages written in Spanish.
cards.explanation: The filter has never seen Spanish, so it needs **Spanish examples**, and **both kinds**: spam only would teach it that Spanish means spam, so friends writing in Spanish would get flagged (like "free" in the pizza message). More English data adds nothing about Spanish.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A model learns only from its **training data**, gaps and all.
- One word, or one example, can tip it the wrong way.
- Better data beats more data: checked, varied and realistic.

Next: how to tell if a model is any good.
